metadata.name: peard_perps
metadata.description: PEARD ASSETS: perpetual futures on anything in the registry, priced by a virtual curve

docs: Perpetual futures on anything the registry can price.
The fourth program, and the one that makes the rest tradeable. peard
says what a thing is worth; this lets somebody be long or short it,
without a warehouse, a deed, a custodian, or anyone willing to take the
other side.
The curve is virtual. Nobody deposits into it and nobody owns a share of
it, so a market opens with no liquidity provider and no counterparty
waiting. Funding is what ties it to reality: when the mark sits above the
index, longs pay shorts, and that payment is what makes being short worth
somebody's while. It is the one mechanism in derivatives that manufactures
its own counterparty, which is exactly why an option on a weekly-printing
pear index does not work and this does.
The honest cost: **the oracle is now in the settlement path.** peard's
core property is that a frozen price stops accrual and never stops
trading. Here the index decides funding and decides who is liquidatable,
so a bad print takes somebody's position. Every path that consumes it
refuses a stale, frozen or expired index rather than working around it,
and refusing halts the book rather than liquidating into a guess.

instructions.name: close_position
docs: Give back size and take the profit or the loss.

instructions.name: cover_bad_debt
docs: Pay a market's shortfall out of the fund.
Permissionless and idempotent: it moves the smaller of what the market
is short and what the fund holds, so a partly funded fund covers part
of the debt now and the rest whenever it is topped up. Nothing here
decides WHO is made whole, because the money goes to the vault rather
than to a person: it restores the pool every open position withdraws
from, which is exactly the thing `bad_debt` said was missing.
`bad_debt` comes down by precisely what arrived. Reducing it by more
would be the same lie in the other direction.

instructions.name: fund_insurance
docs: Put money in. Anyone may, and nobody may take it out again.
There is no withdraw instruction and that is the point: a fund the
operator can drain is not insurance, it is a float. The only way out is
`cover_bad_debt`, which pays a market vault rather than a person.

instructions.name: grant_insurance_credit
docs: Allocate fund the market did not earn, to a market the admin vouches for.
`cover_bad_debt` is capped at `insurance_credit`, which only
`sweep_fees_to_insurance` raises, so a market that has not yet earned
its own buffer could never be covered by a donation. That is right by
default and wrong as an absolute: the point of a shared fund is that a
young market is covered by an older one's fees.
So the sharing is explicit and admin-signed rather than implicit and
permissionless. An attacker's freshly-created market gets nothing
unless a human allocates it something, which is the entire difference
between this and the common pot it replaces. The allocation is a
promise, not a transfer: nothing moves until `cover_bad_debt` finds a
genuine shortfall.

instructions.name: init_insurance
docs: Stand something behind `bad_debt`.
One fund for every market. Admin-created because it is a singleton and
somebody has to pay the rent; everything that moves money afterwards is
permissionless, deliberately. An admin gate on paying a vault back what
it owes traders would be a gate on the wrong side of the transaction.

instructions.name: init_market
docs: Open a market on a registry pairable.
`base_reserve` and `quote_reserve` set the opening mark and, more
importantly, the depth: `k` decides how far a given size moves the
price, and it is the only liquidity parameter there is. Too small and
the market is unusable; too large and the curve will absorb size the
vault cannot cover.

accounts.name: pairable
docs: the caller names, because a market that names the wrong one can
never be created again.

instructions.name: liquidate
docs: Close somebody else's position because it can no longer pay.
Permissionless, and paid out of what is left, which is the only
reason anyone runs a liquidator. Margin is measured against the index
rather than the mark so that pushing the curve cannot manufacture a
liquidation, and a stale index blocks this along with everything
else: a book that cannot be liquidated is bad, and one liquidated
against a number nobody stands behind is worse.

instructions.name: migrate_market
docs: Grow a market or global account created before backing existed.
Permissionless and idempotent. The market seed is
`[b"market", pairable]`, so a market can never be re-created; without
this, the markets already deployed would stop deserialising the moment
the struct grew. Anchor's `realloc` zeroes the new bytes, which is
exactly the unbacked default, so a migrated market behaves precisely
as it did before.

accounts.name: market
docs: precisely what an under-sized account cannot survive. Identity is
proved by discriminator inside, and the program owns it by construction.

instructions.name: open_position
docs: Post collateral and take a side.
`base_delta` is signed: positive goes long, negative short. Adding to
a position is allowed; flipping one is not, because a flip is two
trades and pretending otherwise hides the realised leg.

instructions.name: set_backing_program
docs: Which reserve program a market may be backed by. Admin only.

accounts.name: authority
docs: EITHER the market's own authority OR the global admin.
`market.authority` is whoever called `init_market`, which is
permissionless, and there is no transfer and no revocation for that
seat. Gating the halt on it alone means a stranger who front-ran a
pairable holds a switch over other people's collateral with nobody
above them. The admin is not a co-owner here and cannot take anything;
it can only undo.

instructions.name: set_market_backing
docs: Stop the book. Positions stay, nothing new opens, EXITS STAY OPEN.
`close_position` is exempt on purpose, so this cannot be used to trap
somebody's collateral. Either the market's authority or the global
admin may call it; see `AdminMarket`.
Point a market at a reserve, or unpoint it.
Authority-gated on purpose. `sync_backing` below is permissionless,
which is only safe because the address it may read is pinned here
first. Without this, anyone could stand up their own reserve, name
this market inside it, and take over the open-interest ceiling.
The default pubkey clears the backing and returns the market to being
bounded by `max_open_base` alone.

accounts.name: authority
docs: EITHER the market's own authority OR the global admin.
`market.authority` is whoever called `init_market`, which is
permissionless, and there is no transfer and no revocation for that
seat. Gating the halt on it alone means a stranger who front-ran a
pairable holds a switch over other people's collateral with nobody
above them. The admin is not a co-owner here and cannot take anything;
it can only undo.

instructions.name: set_market_index_age
docs: Widen the window in which a position can still be closed.
This exists because four markets were created with
`max_index_age_secs` exactly equal to their pairable's
`max_price_age_secs`, which leaves no window at all rather than a
narrow one, and nothing else in this program could repair them.
`init_market` now refuses that shape outright, so this is a fix for
what already shipped rather than a parameter anybody should expect to
tune.
It only ever raises. A lower value could take away an exit that a
position is relying on right now, and this instruction must not be
able to create the state it exists to undo. That makes it monotone:
whatever the authority does with it, no open position ends up with a
smaller window than it had.

accounts.name: pairable
docs: exactly as `sync_index` does. The registry's own staleness bound is
read from it, so a market cannot be widened against the wrong account.

instructions.name: settle_funding
docs: Charge one funding interval.
Permissionless, because everyone with a position has a reason to want
it cranked and nobody can steer it: the rate comes entirely from the
gap between mark and index, and the direction from its sign.

instructions.name: settle_market
docs: Freeze the market at the underlying's final price.
Permissionless and one-way. It reads the registry account directly,
and unlike `sync_index` it *requires* the pairable to be past its
expiry: that is precisely the state in which the registry refuses
further pushes, which is what makes the last print final by
construction rather than by anyone deciding it is.
Staleness is deliberately not checked here. Past expiry a price is
not stale, it is finished, and refusing it would leave every position
exactly as stuck as doing nothing.

instructions.name: settle_position
docs: Close one position at the settlement price.
Permissionless, so nobody's exit depends on their own diligence or on
still holding the key that opened it. There is no claim deadline and
nothing expires unclaimed: the position becomes collateral, and
collateral is withdrawable forever.
The curve is not touched. Everyone leaves at the same number, which
is the point of cash settlement and the reason the last one out is
not punished for being last.

instructions.name: sweep_fees_to_insurance
docs: Move a market's accrued fees into the fund.
Fees have always accrued into the market's own vault and nothing has
ever taken them out, so they sit there indefinitely, mixed with
collateral and counted by nothing. Routing them here turns an idle
balance into the thing that backs the book.
The bound is the whole safety argument: a vault holds collateral it
OWES traders plus whatever else has landed in it, and only the excess
may leave. `free = held - collateral_total` is that excess, and
sweeping is capped at it. A market already carrying bad debt therefore
refuses on its own, without a special case, because a vault that is
short of what it owes has no free balance by definition.

instructions.name: sync_backing
docs: Copy the reserve's published figure onto the market.
Permissionless, and it reads a foreign account by hand rather than by
CPI, exactly as `sync_index` reads a pairable. Nothing is trusted but
three pins: the program that owns the account, the address this market
names, and the market the attestation names back. The magic and the
version turn a moved or wrong account into a loud failure instead of
plausible nonsense parsed out of somebody else's bytes.
The attestation's own `as_of` is stored rather than the sync time. A
reserve nobody has marked in a week must look a week old however
recently this was cranked.

accounts.name: backing
docs: market names, and the market the attestation names back.

instructions.name: sync_index
docs: Copy the registry's price onto the market.
Permissionless, and it reads the foreign account by hand: the program
is pinned by governance, the account by the market, and the id inside
has to match the one cached at creation. A registry that is frozen,
unpriced, or past its expiry yields nothing, and the market then
refuses to fund, open, or liquidate until it does.

instructions.name: withdraw_collateral
docs: Take collateral back out. Only down to the initial margin, so
withdrawing cannot be a way to open leverage the market refuses.

types.name: BackingSynced
docs: Worth watching rather than merely logging: this is the number that
bounds how large the market may become, and a fall in it shrinks the
market without anyone deciding to shrink it.

fields.name: remaining
docs: What the market is STILL short after this, so a partial cover is
legible without reading the account back.

fields.name: registry_program
docs: The program whose pairables this one will read prices from. Pinned by
governance, because a market naming its own price source is a market
writing its own liquidation trigger.

fields.name: usd_mint
docs: The one mint positions are collateralised and settled in.

fields.name: backing_program
docs: The program whose reserve attestations a market may be backed by.
Settable, unlike `registry_program` and `usd_mint`, because backing is
an addition rather than a foundation: a cluster runs perfectly well
with this unset, and every market simply stays unbacked.

types.name: Insurance
docs: A perpetual on one registry pairable.
The curve is virtual: no one deposits into it and no one owns a share of
it. Reserves exist only to price size against, which is what lets a
market open with no liquidity provider at all and no counterparty waiting
on the other side. What backs a payout is the collateral vault, and what
keeps the curve honest against the real world is funding.
**This program puts the oracle in the settlement path**, and that is a
deliberate inversion of peard's core property. There, a frozen price
stops accrual and never stops trading. Here, the index decides funding
and decides who is liquidatable, so a bad print costs someone their
position. Every path that consumes the index therefore refuses a stale,
frozen, or expired one rather than working around it.
What stands behind `Market::bad_debt`.
`bad_debt` is the amount a market's vault is short of `collateral_total`,
which is what it owes traders. Nothing stood behind that number, so the
shortfall landed on whoever withdrew last: the vault simply ran out, and
`pay_out` failed with `VaultShort` for whoever was slowest. That is not a
risk anybody agreed to when they deposited.
One fund for every market rather than one each. Bad debt is rare and
lumpy, so a per-market fund is either idle or too small on the day it is
needed, which is the argument for pooling insurance generally.
It never sits in the hot path. `apply_funding` and `liquidate` still
record the shortfall exactly as before, and `cover_bad_debt` moves the
money afterwards. That keeps the code that runs while a position is under
margin pressure unchanged, which is where a new failure mode would be
least welcome and hardest to test.

fields.name: total_funded
docs: Everything ever paid in, from any source. Monotonic.

fields.name: total_covered
docs: Everything ever paid out to cover a market. Monotonic.

fields.name: total_from_fees
docs: The part of `total_funded` swept out of market fee accruals rather
than donated. Kept apart because one is the protocol funding itself
and the other is somebody choosing to.

fields.name: by
docs: A wallet for a donation, the market itself for a fee sweep.

fields.name: pairable
docs: The peard `Pairable` this tracks. Never CPI'd into, only read.

fields.name: pairable_id
docs: Its id, cached so a synced price cannot be swapped for another
pairable's without the mismatch being obvious.

fields.name: base_reserve
docs: Virtual reserves. Base at 9dp, quote at 6dp.

fields.name: k
docs: `base_reserve * quote_reserve`, held constant by every trade. Stored
so a repeg is an explicit act rather than a rounding artefact.

fields.name: index_price
docs: Last synced index price, USD e6, and the pairable's own timestamp for
it. Never the sync time: a registry nobody has pushed to in an hour
should look an hour old however recently somebody cranked this.

fields.name: max_index_age_secs
docs: Past this the index is refused. Funding stops, opens stop, and
liquidation stops with them, which is the safe direction: better a
frozen book than liquidations priced off a number nobody stands
behind.

fields.name: cumulative_funding
docs: Cumulative funding, FUNDING_ONE scaled, in whole quote per whole
unit of base. Not quote e6: `Position::funding_owed` is what puts
the answer back on the scale collateral is kept in, and the two
carrying different scales is the point rather than an oversight.
The same lazy-index trick as peard's roll and floorlaunch's debt:
one number reprices every position, and each one is brought forward
on next touch, so funding is O(1) rather than a walk over the book.

fields.name: max_funding_bps
docs: Cap on one funding step, bps of the index. A single print far from
the mark should not be able to empty a position in one crank.

fields.name: long_base
docs: Open base, 9dp, each side. Their difference is the imbalance funding
is trying to close; their cap is what stops the curve taking more
risk than the vault can carry.

fields.name: collateral_total
docs: Sum of every position's collateral. What the vault owes traders, as
distinct from what it holds.

fields.name: bad_debt
docs: Losses the vault had to absorb because a position closed below zero.
Not a rounding counter: a nonzero figure means liquidation was too
slow at least once, and it belongs in front of anyone depositing.

fields.name: fees_usd
docs: Fees taken, withdrawable to the global fee receiver.

fields.name: fee_bps
docs: Taken on notional at open and at close, bps.

fields.name: maintenance_margin_bps
docs: Collateral floor as a fraction of notional, bps. Below it, the
position may be liquidated by anyone.

fields.name: initial_margin_bps
docs: Collateral required to open, bps of notional. The inverse is max
leverage: 1000bps is 10x.

fields.name: liquidation_fee_bps
docs: Cut of a liquidated position's remaining collateral paid to whoever
closed it, bps. The only reason anyone runs a liquidator.

fields.name: max_divergence_bps
docs: How far mark may sit from index before opens are refused, bps. A
curve that has been walked away from reality should stop taking new
risk before it stops being able to pay.

fields.name: settled
docs: Settlement, for a market on a dated underlying.
A crop year and a futures contract month both stop taking prices at
expiry, and a perpetual on a thing that stopped existing is a
contradiction. Without this the market simply halts: the stored index
ages out, every path that needs it refuses, and positions and their
collateral are trapped for good.
So it settles instead. `settled_price` is the underlying's final
print, which is final by construction rather than by decree, because
the registry refuses pushes past expiry. Everyone leaves at the same
number, nobody races the curve on the way out, and there is no claim
deadline to miss.

fields.name: backing
docs: A reserve of the real thing, if anyone has put one behind this market.
The default pubkey means unbacked, which is what almost every market
is and what every market was before this existed. An unbacked market
behaves exactly as it did: `max_open_base` alone bounds it.
When it IS set, the market can never carry more open interest than
there is real backing for. That turns "backed" from a claim on a
website into an enforced ceiling: pears rot, the reserve marks down,
the cap falls, and the market shrinks without anyone deciding to
shrink it. The seasonality runs the other way too, since cheaper
pears mean more pears behind the same dollars.

fields.name: backing_value_usd
docs: The reserve's marked value, USD e6, copied from its attestation.

fields.name: backing_as_of
docs: The `as_of` the attestation itself carried, NOT when we synced it. A
reserve nobody has marked in a week must look a week old however
recently somebody cranked.

fields.name: backing_max_age_secs
docs: How stale that attestation may be before opens are refused. Closing
is never gated on it: a holder must always be able to leave.

fields.name: funding_pool
docs: Funding collected from the paying side and not yet handed to the
receiving side.
THE THING THAT MAKES FUNDING CONSERVED. `settle_funding` moves one
index and every position applies its own share independently, so
nothing was netting the two sides against each other. Whenever
`long_base != short_base` the payments did not sum to zero, and a
net-long book with the mark below the index credited every long real,
withdrawable collateral that no short had paid in. The vault then owed
more than it held and `pay_out` failed for whoever was slowest, which
is a loss taken by a trader who did nothing wrong.
Now a credit can only draw on what was actually collected. Paying
fills this; receiving empties it; it can never go negative, so the
vault can never promise money nobody paid.

fields.name: funding_unpaid
docs: Funding a receiver was owed and the pool could not cover.
Distinct from `bad_debt`, and the distinction matters. `bad_debt` is
what a PAYER failed to pay. This is what a RECEIVER failed to get
because the other side was smaller or slower. Netting them into one
figure would hide which of the two happened, and they call for
different answers: bad debt wants an insurance fund, an unpaid credit
wants a counterparty.
It is a counter rather than a claim. Nothing pays it out, because
paying it out is exactly the thing that was minting money.

fields.name: insurance_credit
docs: A time-weighted mark, over one funding interval.
FUNDING IS CHARGED AGAINST THIS, NOT THE SPOT CURVE, and that is the
whole reason it exists. `mark_price()` is an instantaneous read of the
reserves, so a trader paying funding could walk the curve onto the
index in one transaction, crank `settle_funding` at a premium of zero,
and restore the position in the next: two swap fees to skip an hour's
funding, repeatable every hour, and the counterparty is paid nothing
for a position that never stopped being one-sided.
Weighted by TIME rather than by trade count, so a mark held for one
slot moves this by one slot's worth of an hour. Anyone can still push
the spot mark anywhere the divergence gate allows; nobody can hold it
there for free.
What THIS market has put into the shared insurance fund, less what
it has drawn back out.
The cap on `cover_bad_debt`, and the reason a stranger's market cannot
empty the fund. `init_market` is permissionless and its parameters are
nearly unbounded, so a market can be built whose vault is genuinely
short by an amount its own creator chose: 10,000x margin, a large long
closing into profit the vault never received, a short closing under
water. Both figures the old cap trusted, `bad_debt` and
`collateral_total - vault`, are then honest by the program's own
definitions and both are as large as the attacker wants.
A market can only ever draw back what it paid in. The fund stops being
a common pot anyone may reach into and becomes a per-market balance
that happens to share a vault.

fields.name: mark_twap_ts
docs: When `mark_twap` last absorbed the standing mark. Zero on a market
migrated in before this field existed, which seeds from spot.

types.name: Position
docs: One trader's position. Signed size, so long and short are one code path.

fields.name: base_size
docs: Base units, 9dp. Positive is long, negative is short, zero is flat.

fields.name: quote_entry
docs: Quote paid in (long) or received (short) to open what is still open,
USD e6. Entry price is this over size.

fields.name: funding_snapshot
docs: Market `cumulative_funding` when this position was last brought
forward. The gap is what it owes or is owed.
